Business Analysis Process Improvement Agile Digital Transformation Product Management Why Your Approval Process Is Slow (and a 6-Step Method to Fix It) Salvador Jimenez Juarez 7 min read · Oct 30, 2026 -- 1 Listen Share A step-by-step Business Analysis method you can apply to any approval workflow that keeps stalling Press enter or click to view image in full size The 6-step method covered in this article For a year and a half, part of my job at a multinational in Mexico City looked like this: open the company platform, create a contract review round, select the reviewers, and submit it for review. Then open the chat group for each country project (like Mexico, or Chile, or Argentina), tag each reviewer by name, and paste the link to the project. Even then, reviews were often slow, and some projects were simply ignored. The review was already waiting in their inbox. Every reviewer could see it on their dashboards and in the chat. But tagging them was how contracts actually moved faster. If you had asked me back then, I would have told you it was a bit absurd — I never liked tagging people in a group where everyone can see it; it felt a little invasive. Everyone should check their own inbox. But I didn’t have the words, or the method, to explain why the process worked that way and how to fix it. But that was simply how everyone did it, so I adopted it too. Years later, during my Master’s at Grenoble École de Management, I wrote a recommendation report about that exact workflow. Recently I turned it into a full Business Analysis case, and I realised that the method behind it works for almost any process that “should be simple but somehow takes forever”: purchase approvals, onboarding, invoice validation, leave requests. Here is the method, step by step, with my real case as the example. Step 1. Describe the problem before anyone suggests a solution The most common mistake in any improvement project is to start with the answer. “We need a new tool.” “Let’s automate it.” Before that, you need a problem statement that everyone agrees on. Write three things: Context: how the process works today, in plain words. Pain points: the symptoms people complain about. Number them (P1, P2, P3…) so you can refer to them later. Root causes: why each symptom happens. In my case, the pain points were easy to list: P1. Reviews stall, so the contract manager tags reviewers in chat groups. P2. When someone votes Disagree , the reason is often missing, so you have to call them to understand it or to clarify their decision. P3. Risk was assessed with an Excel file, the “Risk Table”, and each country applied it differently (in specific situations). The root causes were less obvious. P1 was not about lazy reviewers. It was that follow-up depended on people, not on the system . That changes everything: if you fix the symptom, you hire someone to chase more people. If you fix the cause, you automate the reminder. Tip: for each pain point, ask “why?” until the answer is something you could actually change in the process. Step 2. Draw the scope line Decide where the process starts and where it ends. Everything outside is out of scope , written down explicitly. Mine started when Sales asked for a contract review and ended when the contract was sent for signature. Customer negotiation, contract drafting and what happened at headquarters were out. It is still useful to know what happens outside the scope. But when someone raises it, the answer is simple: “That’s out of scope, and here is who can help.” This sounds bureaucratic, but it protects the project from the sentence every analyst fears: “While we’re at it, could we also…” Step 3. List the stakeholders and decide who decides A stakeholder is anyone affected by the process or able to block the change. If you forget one, they will appear at the end, usually to say no. For each one, note what they want and how much influence they have. Then build a RACI matrix : for every activity, who is: R esponsible: does the work, A ccountable: approves the result and answers for it (only one person per activity), C onsulted: asked for input before the decision, I nformed: told after the decision. Press enter or click to view image in full size RACI extract: one “A” per activity The rule of a single “A” is the most useful one. In my old workflow, backup reviewers existed, but when someone was away, nobody knew who was really supposed to approve. In some cases, the backup didn’t even have permission to review. Two people responsible for the same thing usually means nobody is. Step 4. Map the process as it is, then as it should be This is the heart of the method. As-is: draw the current process, step by step, including the workarounds nobody talks about. In my map, “contract manager tags reviewers in the country chat group” is a real step, because it was part of the routine. Colour the painful steps in red . Press enter or click to view image in full size As-is: red steps are the pain points To-be: draw the improved process . Colour the changes in blue . Then compare the two maps side by side: anyone should see what disappears and what is new. Press enter or click to view image in full size To-be: blue steps are the changes A detail that only the as-is map revealed: our process ran in rounds .
